implementation_notes: A Kotlin data class generates `copy(...)` with defaults for every primary-constructor property, so one level of update is an expression and depth nests: `p.copy(home = p.home.copy(city = "Berlin"))`, which replaces the hand-written copy cascade with compiler-generated code and `val` properties make accidental writes impossible. Storing, passing or deriving the path is still not possible with `copy` alone, so the classic composed form (hand-written getter/setter lambdas, or Arrow Optics) is justified exactly when the same deep focus is reused across many call sites or must travel as data.
pitfalls: `copy()` is shallow: mutable collections and arrays held by the data class are shared between the copies, so a "new" value can still be mutated through the old one - use persistent collections or defensively copy.
Only primary-constructor properties participate: state stored in the body (or in a superclass's mutable field) is not covered by `copy` and can desynchronise from it.
Equality is generated from the primary constructor properties only, so a data class with significant body state compares equal while behaving differently.

variants.name: Arrow Optics Lens with the @optics compiler plug-in
variants.implementation_notes: Arrow Optics models the lens explicitly: `Lens<Person, String>` exposes `get`, `set` and `modify`, composes with the infix `compose`, and the KSP-based `@optics` compiler plug-in derives the optics alongside the data class and adds dot-syntax extension functions so `Person.home.city` reads and updates as a focus. It is the standard optics library in the Kotlin ecosystem and reads best when a model has many deep foci or when optics are generated for a whole schema; for a single nested update, the plain `copy()` chain stays shorter and needs no plug-in in the build.
pitfalls: The generated lenses need the KSP plug-in in the build and a `companion object` on every annotated class (the beta Arrow Optics Gradle plug-in removes both requirements); without them the dot-syntax simply does not resolve and the failure looks like an ordinary compile error.

Optics are generated at compile time, so a focus on a renamed or removed field breaks the build until the optics are regenerated - failing loudly is the point, but it couples model edits to annotation processing.
`@optics` requires the annotated type to be a data class (or a sealed hierarchy for prisms); value classes and plain classes need hand-written optics.
